issues.issue: The phrase "some other evidence of deficiency which COMPANY shall specify, including but not limited to products received with less than sixty (60) days of remaining shelf life" is garbled: the sixty-day item is a category of defective product, not a form of evidence. It is unclear whether short shelf life is itself a ground for credit or merely proof of one.

Credit is made to depend on "policies and standards set and established from time to time by COMPANY," which conflicts with 15(iii)'s requirement that the Agreement be modified only by mutual written instrument and with 7(i)'s stated rejection right. The unilateral policy power can defeat the express remedy.

The proviso excluding "PRODUCTS ... manufactured by DISTRIBUTOR and shipped under DISTRIBUTOR'S labels" cannot be squared with Section 1(ii), which defines PRODUCTS as goods authorized by COMPANY for sale to DISTRIBUTOR, or with 3(ii)(e) under which COMPANY supplies them. The carve-out appears to describe a transaction this Agreement does not contain.

"COMPANY shall supply" is immediately qualified by "at COMPANY'S sole discretion" and "as may be available to COMPANY," so the sentence states both a duty and an unfettered discretion not to perform it. The catch-all in (d), "such other promotional information and assistance as may be available," compounds the indefiniteness.

The bar on using "any packing materials, descriptive literature, advertising, etc." without prior written consent conflicts with 3(ii)(v), which makes DISTRIBUTOR "solely responsible for any and all promotions, sales and marketing programs, advertising." One clause gives control, the other assigns sole responsibility.

"[T]he General market information regarding the TERRITORY" is undefined and capitalised inconsistently, giving no boundary to what must be handed over on request. The obligation is short but its content is unascertainable.

The confidentiality duty covers "any and all business and technical information pertaining to the COMPANY and/or the PRODUCTS" with no carve-out for publicly available or independently obtained information and no time limit. The open-ended "includes but is not limited to" leaves the protected category unbounded.

"[G]ood cause" is defined as breach "not cured within those times specified below," yet the clause simultaneously requires ninety days' written notice, so it is unclear whether the ninety days runs before or after the cure period. "[A] change in COMPANY's business that results in COMPANY no longer using Independent DSDD distributors in this territory" is a further undefined trigger resting entirely on COMPANY's own conduct.

Requiring good cause and ninety days' notice cannot be reconciled with Section 2, which lets either party terminate on ninety days' notice without any cause, nor with 12(ii) and 12(iii), which permit immediate termination or termination after a five-business-day cure period. The three termination regimes give inconsistent answers to the same facts.

"Make a material change in the control of DISTRIBUTOR'S company that is unacceptable to COMPANY" makes the trigger turn on COMPANY's unexpressed subjective judgment, and neither "material change in control" nor "unacceptable" is defined. Item (f)'s "threatens to do substantial harm to the COMPANY'S business or commercial reputation" is equally open.

Immediate termination for an attempted assignment sits against 15(ii)(a), which declares any such attempted assignment simply "void and without effect," and against 12(i)'s definition of good cause as an uncured breach requiring ninety days' notice. The remedies for the same act differ across the instrument.

The clause gives "five (5) business days written notice" and then measures the cure by "said five (5) day period," so it is unclear whether the cure window is five business days or five calendar days. The difference determines whether a termination was premature.

A five-day cure followed by termination cannot be squared with 12(i), which requires ninety days' written notice for termination for good cause defined by reference to these very cure periods. Section 2's ninety-day notice compounds the mismatch.

The parenthetical exempting "isolated, but not systemic" failures to remove out-of-date merchandise unless they occur more than six times is inserted in the middle of the two-strikes proviso, so it is unclear which rule governs a repeated service failure. "[I]solated, but not systemic" is itself an unmeasured distinction.

Termination for failures that are material "in the sole discretion of COMPANY" after a five-day cure conflicts with 12(i)'s requirement of ninety days' notice for good cause and with Section 2's notice period. It also cross-refers to "(i), (ii), or (iti)(a)" using a mis-typed numeral.

The sentence closes with a stray "for.)." and its repurchase price, "DISTRIBUTOR'S net warehouse cost," is not defined anywhere in the Agreement. What deductions or freight are included in that cost is left open.

The obligation to hand back "free of charge" all products COMPANY previously supplied at no charge sits against 4(iii), under which all PRODUCTS are sold to DISTRIBUTOR "absolutely" with title passing on delivery. Which goods fall on each side of that line is unclear.

The clause says neither party "shall be liable ... for any consequential, punitive or incidental damages ... in any cumulative amount greater than" 50% of a year's gross sales, which reads either as an outright exclusion or as a cap permitting such damages up to that figure. The two readings are irreconcilable and decide whether lost profits are recoverable at all.

If read as a cap it conflicts with Section 13(i)'s unqualified indemnity for "any and all claims, demands, costs, expenses ... and liabilities or losses" caused by breach, and with 7(i)'s sole-remedy provision. The instrument gives no ordering rule between them.

The self-help repossession right "without the need for any further consent or notice" sits against 12(iv)'s repurchase machinery and 4(iii)'s absolute passing of title, and gives no standard for when indebtedness is due. The clauses are reconcilable but their interaction on termination is untested.

The two-year period runs from when "the harm that gave rise to the cause of action arose," a trigger different from accrual and undefined for continuing or later-discovered harm. When the clock starts is exactly the sort of question this wording invites.

The limitation period interacts with 12(v), which measures damages by gross sales "in the twelve months immediately preceding the date upon which an action or proceeding is commenced," but the two use different reference dates. No provision reconciles them.

An indemnity covering losses caused "by a breach of this Agreement by ... the indemnifying party" makes each party indemnify the other for first-party breach damages, which cannot easily be squared with the 12(v) limitation on liability or 7(i)'s sole-remedy clause. Whether the indemnity overrides the damages cap is unresolved.
The mutual insurance obligation is asymmetric in its excess-coverage and certificate requirements, but nothing in the instrument contradicts it. The dollar amounts are specific and self-executing.

The audit right is exercisable "at reasonable times and in its sole discretion" while access is "limited to services performed for COMPANY," yet the record-keeping duty covers "all of its operations and transactions relating to this Agreement." The scope of records that must actually be produced is therefore uncertain.

The effective-date sentence provides only for receipt "by mail, if sent only by mail service, or facsimile," leaving personal service and overnight courier — both authorised methods in the same clause — with no stated effective date. That gap matters directly to the ninety-day and five-day notice periods elsewhere.

Because the notice machinery does not fix an effective date for courier or personal delivery, its interaction with the strict notice periods in Section 2 and Section 12 is left open. Whether a validly served notice started the clock could turn on this omission.

The clause slips into first person — "an assignment effected with our prior written consent" — in an agreement that otherwise refers to COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR, leaving the consenting party identified only by inference. It also declares attempted assignments both "void and without effect" and "a material breach," which are inconsistent characterisations.

Treating any attempted assignment as void conflicts with 12(ii)(a), which treats the same act as a ground for immediate termination with consent "not to be unreasonably withheld," and with 15(ii)(a)'s express permission to use subdistributors. The instrument gives three different consequences for transfers of the distributorship.

The consent standard is self-cancelling: COMPANY "will not unreasonably withhold" consent but it "will not be unreasonable" to impose the listed conditions "among other requirements," an open-ended catch-all that can swallow the reasonableness promise. The clause also lapses into "we" and "us" without defining those pronouns.

Condition 5, under which execution of a new DSDD Agreement "will terminate this Agreement," adds a termination route absent from Section 12's otherwise comprehensive termination provision and from Section 2's successor-agreement mechanism. Whether an assignment can terminate the Agreement outside Section 12 is unresolved.

Permission to conduct business through subdistributors conflicts with 15(ii)(a), which treats DISTRIBUTOR's services as personal and voids any transfer of the Agreement "in whole or in part," and with 3(ii)(a)(iii)(A), which forbids wholesaler operations where in-store service is not given to individual outlets. Whether using independent distributors is permitted or a material breach is genuinely open.

COMPANY's free right to assign is the mirror opposite of the elaborate restrictions imposed on DISTRIBUTOR in the same subsection, but the asymmetry is expressly stated rather than contradictory. Nothing elsewhere qualifies it.

The requirement that modification be "only by a written instrument duly executed by the parties" cannot be reconciled with 3(ii)(d), which lets COMPANY revise Exhibit B "from time to time without notice in the sole discretion of COMPANY," nor with 3(ii)(b) and Section 4's unilateral changes to policies, prices and terms. Exhibits are expressly part of the Agreement under 15(vii).
The non-agency provision duplicates Section 1(i) and adds a further indemnity, overlapping with 3(ii)(v) and 13(i) without any priority rule. The overlap is cumulative rather than contradictory.
Delaware law is chosen although neither party is located there and performance is in New York and neighbouring states, which could raise a choice-of-law challenge. The clause itself is unambiguous.

The merger clause is qualified by "except as otherwise expressly provided herein" without identifying any such exception, leaving the reach of the supersession open. Its scope is limited to "the subject matter thereof," itself undefined.

The clause supersedes all prior agreements between the parties, yet 3(ii) settles claims arising under a November 14, 2006 writing and preserves accrued credits owed by COMPANY. Whether those pre-existing obligations survive the merger clause is a genuine question.
"[E]ach of which shall be deemed the original" should read "an original"; taken literally it makes every counterpart the single original. The error has no practical consequence.

The TERRITORY — the central grant of the Agreement — is handwritten and substantially illegible ("Py, N'T) PA, Cann."), so the states covered cannot be determined from the document. Whether the territory extends to whole states or parts of them is likewise unstated.

Exhibit A purports to fix the TERRITORY, but 3(i) gives COMPANY the right to "determine the TERRITORY" unilaterally during the term and 3(ii)(c) says DISTRIBUTOR has no exclusive rights to any designated geography. The exhibit's grant and the operative text pull in opposite directions.

The excluded channels are given almost entirely by "e.g." examples and undefined trade categories such as "Specialty stores," "Chain Warehouse programs" and "Mid tier stores," leaving the boundary of each class to argument. Whether a given retailer falls inside an exclusion cannot be read off the list.

The carve-out permitting distribution to Kmart contradicts the exclusion of "Mass merchandisers" in the same line and cannot be squared with Section 1(iii), which limits sales to "retail grocery store outlet customers only." Kmart is both permitted and outside the authorized channel of trade.

The grandfather runs "until further notice from COMPANY" and covers "any of its customers as of the date hereof," neither of which fixes a determinable set of accounts or an end date. Whether an account existed "as of the date hereof" and what notice suffices are both left open.

Permitting continued sales into excluded channels contradicts 3(ii)(d), which flatly prohibits selling to the customers and channels on Exhibit B and makes any such sale a breach subject to termination, and Section 1(iii)'s grocery-only limitation. The exception and the prohibition cover the same conduct.

Exhibit C is titled "DSDD INDEMNIFICATION" and is required by 15(ii)(a) under that name, yet it contains no indemnity obligation at all, only acknowledgments and disclaimers. What a subdistributor is actually undertaking is therefore uncertain.

The prohibition turns on effects "as determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," making the standard of breach entirely subjective and unreviewable on its face. The open-ended "nor fail to take any actions" has no boundary.

Kellogg's direct-sales right is limited "to the extent permitted by the agreement then in effect between Kellogg and Premier," yet 3(i) and 3(ii)(k) of that agreement give Kellogg unrestricted rights to sell in the territory. The cross-reference makes the limitation empty.
The sentence reads "the composition of the goods constitution Products," a garbled phrase that obscures what Kellogg may change. The meaning is recoverable but the words as written do not state it.

The disclaimer reads "a third party beneficiary or any agreement," where "of" is plainly intended; as written the sentence does not say what the subdistributor is disclaiming. The error is obvious on its face.

The restriction operates only where the expansion has an effect "as determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," so whether conduct breaches the clause depends entirely on one party's unexpressed judgment. No objective standard is supplied.

The clause reads "between the terms and conditions set forth herein as those set forth in any such agreement," where "and" is plainly meant, leaving the comparison ungrammatical. The intended sense is nevertheless clear.

Exhibit C makes its own terms override any Premier–subdistributor agreement, but 15(vii) of the main Agreement provides that this Agreement with its exhibits is the entire agreement between COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR, and 15(ii)(a) permits subdistribution generally. Which instrument governs a conflict touching all three parties is not addressed.
